body.text: Twelve years into three back-to-back BJP governments, much has been written about the political and electoral character of the saffron party. In Spectacle State, academic Brahma Prakash looks instead at the aesthetics and perceptual politics of Hindutva.

Prakash, who teaches theatre and performance studies at JNU’s School of Arts and Aesthetics, writes in his prologue: “Hindutva is more about experiencing than the ideology.” The book covers that experience across material, aural, visual, emotional, and sensory registers. It works both as an introduction and as a more detailed study, approaching Hindu majoritarian politics from angles that get less attention. Prakash traces a range of Hindutva markers—from bulldozers to angry Hanuman stickers to H-pop—looking at how they emerged and what role they play in the aesthetic politics of fascist and far-right movements. Prakash’s previous works are Cultural Labour: Conceptualizing the ‘Folk Performanc’ in India and Body on the Barricades: Life, Art and Resistance in Contemporary India.

Spectacle State is written in a journalistic style rather than a strictly academic one. Instead of explaining the politics of our time through a single leader, personality, or ideology, Prakash looks at the everyday forms Hindutva takes. Speaking to Frontline, Prakash discusses the cultural reach of the Hindutva machinery, which he traces to Sanatana Dharma as much as to capital. Neoliberalism, he says, has sped up how openly Hindutva’s spectacles now appear.
Edited excerpts
Where would you locate the Hindutva spectacle in the global architecture of right-wing spectacle? Is it the same fascist aesthetic, or does Hindutva’s religious character make it different?

Hindutva spectacle captures a range of things, various images and spectacles that I try to capture in my book. It ranges from bulldozer to sword, statue to monument, music, and fashion, from a big statue to a small sticker. Some of them are part of the global architecture of the right—better to say far-right. But I would like to slightly shift the gaze. For me, Hindutva is fundamentally a programme of counter-revolution, to use B.R. Ambedkar’s term, and counter-cultural revolution against the oppressed castes and communities in India.

I write in Spectacle State how we cannot miss the counter-revolution that remains the core of fascist ideologies and impacts all sorts of relationships in the longer run—of property, gender, race, caste. The attack on Muslims is quite evident, but reducing the Hindutva project to the attack or othering of Muslims or minorities is not enough. It is also about withdrawing the basic rights of the majority—Bahujans. I write: the far-right movement is leading to a massive curtailment of rights and freedom, more directly of the minorities but also of majority others, including women, Dalits, Bahujans, and Adivasi communities. Every single Hindutva assault on Muslims also carries the direct or indirect assault on the questions of social justice. W.E.B. Du Bois tells us that such backlashes from the privileged sections happen after every radical and democratic transformation.

Hindutva spectacles were very much there, but neoliberalism—many times in dormant forms and certain emotional bonds—has accelerated the pace and process in which they have come out open and become more visible. They have become more potent and visible with new media and technologies and stand in dialogue with the global architecture of far-right spectacle. When we see Hindutva only as part of that global architecture, we miss its foundation in caste society that nurtures its soul and sustains its goal.

The ideology of Hindu and Brahmanical supremacy has been there before the advent of liberalism and neoliberalism. We get a fuller picture when we also account for its counter-revolutionary project. Hindutva is turning Muslim subjects into spectacle, but we should not miss how it sharpened its attacks and programmes after the Mandal movement. The RSS newspaper Organiser wrote something quite remarkable: an urgent need to build up moral and spiritual forces to counter any fallout from an expected Shudra rebellion. Exposing this relationship is core to the book. It comes more prominently when I discuss the sword and how we interpret its resurgence in recent years. To create spectacle? To terrorise Muslims? That is not enough. The resurgence of swords is also there to reinstall Brahmin-Kshatriya domination.

There are several other factors that make the Hindutva spectacle unique. One is the living cultural practices of myths and festivals in India that give it easy ground to orchestrate available materials without losing their old efficacious and symbolic values. Second is the massive network of the Sangh Parivar and their “seva” in a caste society. They have years of work behind them, allowed to operate under the nose of all political outfits, from the Congress to the CPI(M). Similar work by other organisations has been seen with far greater suspicion—think of comparable efforts by Muslim or Christian organisations, or more radical Maoist ones. This was possible partly because, as Thomas Blom Hansen has discussed, Hindutva was able to become the hegemonic frame of reference for talking about nation, culture, and seva.

Recent movements like the CJP have shown that there are cracks in the Hindutva spectacle for a different kind of politics to emerge. But we also see the BJP quickly regrouping to win back Gen Z’s imagination. Do spectacles exhaust themselves? How long can capital substitute for consent?

Call it cracks, dents, or shattering of the most consecrated image, but the recent CJP movement has done something remarkable. It has exposed the image and spectacle that Hindutva so carefully crafted for years. The political power of Hindutva is massively dented by the strike of cockroaches, though its hegemony remains at large. Even to reverse it will take a long time, and the resistance perhaps has to enter everyday life—food, festivals, clothing, alternative imagining. The BJP and Sangh outfits are feeling flustered and frustrated after Jantar Mantar; they’re going all out to save the cultic aura.

In despair, they are repeating old theatrics that aren’t working. They will carry out the backlash at every possible level. The spectacle is not just about spectacle—it is detrimental to its political survival. Any spectacle’s power lies in its constant performance and its capacity to mobilise others. It would be difficult to say how long capital can substitute for consent. Guy Debord observed long ago that spectacle is part of the capitalist relationship—in capitalism, we are already in the society of the spectacle. In his view, the spectacle is not a collection of images but a social relation between people mediated by image.

For Debord, spectacle was a sign of a totalising capitalist system, so with surplus, spectacles cannot be exhausted. In that extreme interpretation, the scope for alternative politics becomes almost impossible. Other scholars have seen spectacles in relation to consent and dissent. The Hindutva spectacle is there to capture our consent; the Jantar Mantar assembly can be read as a counter-spectacle of dissent. The problem in India is that caste and Hinduism make spectacles more durable and performative. They don’t necessarily need innovation—repetition gives them a sense of authenticity and ritualised legitimacy.

In the chapter “Dance of the Bulldozer,” you describe Hindutva as a “poor fascist” when it comes to access to machines that provide speed and hyper-mobility, unlike Italian fascism and contemporary Zionism. Yet Hindutva enjoys massive corporate backing. Is it a deliberate aesthetic choice, or is Hindutva able to command capital but not convert it like the former did?

My label of Hindutva as a poor fascist is a rhetorical one. But it is also true that Hindutva remains poor, both in resources and materiality. I make a distinction between the fascist and futurist obsession with steel and speed—Italian fascism and contemporary Zionism are far ahead in terms of style and investment. Compared to them, Hindutva is backward. It has massive corporate backing, but that hasn’t come down to the mass level. Take this appalling example: the Hindutva ecosystem has produced a toy bulldozer, unlike the Zionist case, where a new bulldozer has been invented and named Dubi—Teddy Bear. I will not say Hindutva is commanding capital; it is capital that is commanding Hindutva. Many times, Hindutva maintains a poor aesthetic as a deliberate choice, to address historical and symbolic anxiety. At Hindutva’s massive rallies and processions, the cadres don’t even have proper outfits—they wield and move sticks like swords. Compared to Zionists and European fascists, Hindutva is poor.
You write that far-right theatre in India is not only attacking theatre’s radical legacy but also subverting its forms by emptying them out. Could you elaborate with examples?

There were right-wing elements in Indian theatre earlier too—one can give examples of “nationalist plays”. But when I talk about far-right theatre, I mean something where the current far-right theatre is completely subverting the grammar of theatre, where one isn’t sure if they’re watching theatre or a photoshopped event. I want to make a distinction between right-wing theatre and far-right theatre. Right-wing theatre will still use the elements of theatre; far-right theatre fundamentally aims to hollow out those forms. Basic theatre elements become unrecognisable. So I talk about a counter-theatre aesthetic of Hindutva that attacks the very ideals and forms of the critical-creative and dialogic spheres of theatre.

Unlike right-wing theatre, far-right theatre posits a crisis at the level of ideology and aesthetics—the very model of theatre. The Marathi play Me Nathuram Godse Boltoy [I Am Nathuram Speaking] is an example of right-wing theatre that still carries the idea and model of theatre. But so-called plays like Operation Sindoor or Lo Ai Wapas Sone ki Chidiya [See, the Bird Has Come Back] are examples of far-right theatre. They are rather photoshopped images and spectacles in which the art of theatre is getting hollowed out.

We also see women’s active participation in Hindutva’s spectacle politics—from the 2020 JNU violence to the anti-reservation protests now. How do we interpret patriarchy within the Indian right-wing framework, where women gain power by enforcing caste and communal boundaries?

Various studies map out the role of women in Hindutva organisations and their active participation—the works of Tanika Sarkar and Kalyani Menon, for instance—but my concern in the book is slightly different. I’m less interested in whether they are cadres or not; for me, it’s how they are participating in and contributing to the social culture of fascism. They are Hindutva women not because they are cadres, but because the ideals of Hindutva womanhood are becoming part of the cultural hegemony. When I talk about the counter-revolution and backlash of Hindutva, it very much implicates women too. A woman can become mardani, but she cannot have an independent existence.

There has been an increasing masculinisation of the Indian public sphere under Hindutva. It carries a deep fear of gender ideology, very much like other global far-right movements—this is what Judith Butler discusses in Who’s Afraid of Gender? So “love jihad” is very much part of the anti-Muslim campaign, but it cannot be seen outside the patriarchal control of Hindu women. In the chapter on lynching, I discuss the circulation of popular tableaux based on the 2022 Shraddha Walkar murder case. Hindutva outfits like the Bajrang Dal showcased it to mobilise Hindus against Muslims—dismembered life-sized dolls, a fridge splashed with red paint. Some tableaux showed the murdered woman wearing a Western dress, suggesting that such clothing invites transgression and sexual violence. In another case, a broken mannequin wore a sari and bindi to show that even traditional, innocent Hindu women can fall into the trap of Muslim men.

If Hindutva operates through the capture of feeling, what might a Left counter-politics of feeling look like? Can there be a counter-spectacle different from the Right’s style, or is the Left forced to fight on the same terrain?

We cannot undermine the role of feeling and emotion in the politics of the Right, the Left, or any other section. Antonio Gramsci pointed out long ago that “the intellectual’s error consists in believing that one can know without understanding and even more without feeling and being impassioned […] that is, without feeling the elementary passions of the people.” Hindutva is orchestrating the elementary passions of the people, both at the level of individual feeling and collective passion, where participants willingly give their consent. It creates a culture of submission and servitude in support of authority. Organisations critical of Hindutva cannot leave the ground of feeling and passion—they must engage with the elementary passions of the people to create a culture of dissent and resistance.
For ideological reasons, Hindutva should have chosen classical or traditional music for mobilisation and propaganda. How and why did it choose pop music?

Hindutva choosing classical or traditional music would look natural, because it also claims to defend the ideals of culture and tradition, tracing Indian classical music to the glorious Vedic past. The paradox can be seen in Bal Thackeray’s choice of inviting Michael Jackson. Thackeray inviting Jackson, and Hindutva dancing to electronic DJ and pop, looks so strange, but that is indeed the case—even though one might assume they’d stick to jagran and bhakti songs. I think Hindutva is more interested in reaching the level of the body, emotion, instinct, vibe. So it moved to music and festivals that create that kind of ground. Second, H-pop is more open and participatory, unlike classical music—it mobilises people at the level of body, passion, and feeling, and helps create an orchestrated order.

In the chapter “Why Does Hindutva Need the Sword”, you write that with a sword in hand, a democratically elected leader starts behaving like a Kshatriya king. Even leaders of parties like the DMK, which have ideologically opposed the BJP, have displayed swords in the past. Is there a Kshatriya ideal that dominates political imagination across the country?

The sword is a weapon as well as a heritage and cultural artefact—part of pride, valour, and possession across cultures—but its massive resurgence in India is quite telling. I discuss one dimension of it in relation to the reinstallment of Kshatriya values, though swords also carry other religious and cultural significance depending on context. Dalit grooms riding horses and displaying swords is very different from Hindutva followers displaying swords in marches and processions. Yet sword values can become a trap in which even the lower orders want to behave like Kshatriyas. I agree that there is a Kshatriya ideal and conquering ideology that dominates political imagination across the country. Because those ideals remain at a subconscious level, it becomes easier for Hindutva to give them Kshatriya expression and mobilise people, including subaltern communities.

The swords of Tipu Sultan, Razia Sultan, and Guru Gobind Singh carry very different connotations. I am largely talking about the current resurgence of swords, which is inherently coloured by Hindutva ideology.

In the book, you write that “Hindutva is not an aberration in Hinduism, but it is the religion in its true Sanatani sense.” But over a decade into BJP rule, how do we understand the consistent efforts from a section of non-BJP voices, including the opposition, to establish a difference between the two? Is that, within the framework of your book, an aesthetic choice, or an existential one for non-BJP entities?

The book often carries a passionate, polemical, rhetorical tone. Many times I use it to counter the very hatred of Hindutva—I deploy rhetoric against rhetoric, provocation against evocative performance. I am not a historian, nor fully a social scientist; my writing is full of frustration, polemic, and provocation. It should not be read literally but with a pinch and a punch. Yet your question stands. There is a section of scholars who think other parties have not engaged with Hinduism—who almost believe these parties haven’t done enough for Hindus and have therefore made the majority unhappy. Unfortunately, these parties and leaders start talking in the same language as Hindutva. Rahul Gandhi has done it; Akhilesh Yadav keeps doing it. Some Left leaders and organisations fall into the same trap too. Unless the opposition takes up anti-caste politics and the project of social transformation, it will keep hiding its own majoritarian presence within Brahminical Hinduism. In the name of polity and culture, Hindutva maintains a false claim of majority, when it is actually full of fractures. Aesthetics and culture are sites of contestation, but they are also about finding an alternative.
